content: The majority of true relapses are expected to occur within the first 6 to 12 months following the completion of treatment. If the follow-up period is truncated to ensure equivalent timeframes for comparison between groups, events occurring after the cut-off point (censor date) may be excluded. For instance, censoring follow-up at 72 weeks would classify participants who initially achieved treatment success but relapsed after 72 weeks as having treatment success at 72 weeks, despite their subsequent relapse. To assess the impact of this potential misclassification, additional sensitivity analyses will be conducted to compare outcomes at later time points, where feasible. However, longer follow-up periods generally result in fewer participants being available, leading to reduced precision in the estimates. The World Health Organization (WHO) consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis treatment, specifically for drug-resistant tuberculosis, were updated in 2022. For comparisons where follow-up times differ between cohorts, it may be necessary to reduce the follow-up time for one cohort to ensure comparability. For example, when comparing the 24or 72-week cohorts from the PRACTECAL study with cohorts that have longer follow-up periods, the proportion of relapses in the longer regimens may be underestimated relative to the shorter regimens. A shorter follow-up duration has the advantage of including a larger proportion of participants in the analysis, potentially increasing precision. However, fewer relapses or deaths may be reported, which could reduce precision. The 72-week cohort from the PRACTECAL study will be used for primary analyses, as the median follow-up period in the comparator regimen is at least 72 weeks. This duration is considered equivalent to 18 months of follow-up for other cohorts. For cohorts with a median follow-up time of less than 72 weeks, outcomes will be compared at 6 and/or 12 months. Where possible, additional sensitivity analyses will evaluate outcomes with 24and 108-week follow-up periods. Figures illustrating the approaches to follow-up time have been constructed for the PICO questions, with accompanying comments justifying the choice of primary and secondary analyses. Relapse data for the South African regimen were derived from the EDRWeb database, while mortality data were obtained by linking the South African death register with the EDRWeb database. Both datasets have similar follow-up approaches, with up to 12 to 24 months of follow-up data available, making misclassification likely to be non-differential between groups. The primary analysis will focus on 24 months of follow-up, with a sensitivity analysis performed for 12 months of follow-up. For the WHO IPD cohort, follow-up times vary, and most datasets do not report relapse data, potentially leading to an underestimation of relapse rates. Follow-up for the South African cohort will be censored at 24 months, including mortality and relapse data. Sensitivity analyses will evaluate outcomes for those who reached 24 months and end-of-treatment outcomes at 18 months for those who completed at least 18 months of treatment. In the NEXT study, follow-up time for the intervention group was at least 24 months. A small proportion of participants in the NEXT standard-of-care (SOC) group had follow-up beyond 24 months post-treatment commencement. Data will be censored at 24 months for consistency between arms. The primary analysis will be conducted at 12 months, with sensitivity analyses performed at 18 and 24 months. The PRACTECAL study's pre-specified primary outcome is evaluated at 72 weeks after treatment initiation, including participants whose data were available at the time of the Guideline Development Group. The 72-week follow-up includes substantially more participants than the 108-week (2-year) follow-up. The comparator regimen has either short (36-week) or long (72-week) follow-up, with most participants completing treatment before 72 weeks. Approximately two-thirds of those completing treatment in the SOC arm have follow-up to 108 weeks.
